title: How dogmatism can impact your training results
summary: NH criticises lifters who tie their ego to a method and, when it fails, either cope or flip to denouncing it while hyping their new method. Using his own ego-driven reaction to a subscriber's critique of his cheat rows, he argues for self-reflection, confident but open-minded training, and taking from others only what fits you (the overlap 'C' zone).

claims.claim: Many lifters attach their ego, experience and reputation to a training standard; when it turns out to be bad, they cope rather than admit they were wrong, which is toxic and hinders progress.
Cheating is an art: cheat reps must be done a certain way and serve a purpose.

A subscriber pointed out his cheat rows had drifted into a form that wasn't serving him; his first reaction was ego-driven defensiveness with fallacious arguments, and it took days to accept he was wrong. He then changed the form to grow again.
Without that correction he might have pushed his cheat rows to 405 for sets of 12 for nothing, because the movement wasn't doing what it was supposed to.
Self-reflection, objectively assessing whether what you do helps you, is a key skill for bodybuilders and athletes.
Changing your mind doesn't mean what you did before was wrong in general, only that it was wrong for you.
The 'everything I do now is great, everything I stopped or don't do is terrible' mindset blocks evolution, since the new method may not work either.
Don't take advice from people with a track record of dogmatic investment in one training style who can't accept that other styles work too.
Be confident in your training but keep watching details for improvements; too open a mind that switches programs constantly is also a problem.
He grows from and loves high volume, but doesn't claim everyone should; some respond better to intensity.

His bias is that hypertrophy is well approached by always increasing tonnage, which implies increasing volume, done differently per individual: some recover from long sessions, others need shorter ones.
Consume YouTube fitness and books not to absorb everything but, once you know who you are and what you want, to spot the overlapping 'C' area of ideas that actually apply to you.

Constantly denouncing your old ways while calling the new ones the best ever is 'turning your jacket', not evolving; truly changing your mind means being able to say good things about what you abandoned.
Natural lifters need to be mentally as well as physically prepared to progress.
